name: Aqua Net

lead: Aqua Net is an American aerosol hairspray created by Rayette of St. Paul, Minnesota, in the 1950s. It holds hair in place with a strong, stiff finish, which made it a staple for bouffants and beehives and later for the big hair of the 1980s.
The appearance payoff is lasting volume and shape: teased, swept-up or sculpted styles stay in place through the day.

paras: People spray it onto dry styled hair to fix a finished look. It is used in salons and at home for retro hairstyles, punk and metal looks and stage styling, and some users also use it for craft and costume purposes.

Like other aerosol sprays it should be used in ventilated areas and away from flames and eyes. Past formulations have drawn attention for ingredients: vinyl chloride as a propellant in the early 1970s and phthalates reported in 2002.

angle.text: Aqua Net locks a finished hairstyle in place. People use it for height and volume in teased or swept-up styles and for sculpted punk, metal and retro looks.

lead: Aqua Net is a hairspray brand made by Rayette of St. Paul, Minnesota, in the 1950s. Sources differ on whether it reached the public in 1953 or 1961. [1]

It suited the bouffant and beehive styles of the 1950s and 1960s, and in the 1980s it became synonymous with big hair, glam rock and hair metal acts such as Mötley Crüe and Cinderella. Ronnie Spector of The Ronettes said, "We used a lot of Aqua Net." [1]
Ownership passed to Unilever in February 1989, to Lornamead in 2006 and later to Meiyume; Lornamead was acquired by Li & Fung in 2012. [1]
infobox: Dimethyl ether, SD alcohol 40-B, aminomethyl propanol

paras: Chemist Raymond E. Lee founded Rayette in 1935, and the company created Aqua Net in the 1950s. Mark Arend and George Barrie took over Rayette in 1959, and Barrie ran an aggressive marketing campaign; Rayette bought Fabergé in 1963. Unilever acquired the brand in 1989. In 2006 Lornamead bought it and rebranded with revived original design elements. [1]

The Three Stooges endorsed the product in the 1960s, and Donna Mills advertised it in the 1980s. It appears in the films After Hours (1985) and When Harry Met Sally... (1989), and an agency pitches for the account in a 2009 episode of Mad Men. Punk musicians including Lars Fredriksen and Michelle Cruz Gonzales used it. [1]
Vinyl chloride, linked to higher risk of certain liver cancers, was used as a propellant in 1970 to 1972. Reports in 2002 said the product contained dibutyl and diethyl phthalate. [1]
It has also been used as a fixative for microbiology stains and charcoal or pastel art, to stiffen crinolines and tulle, and as a 3D-printing adhesion aid. [1]
